concept: MongoDB Atlas Agent Engine: memory service, agent runtime, features and SDK
summary: Source-anchored research for MongoDB Atlas Agent Engine: memory service, agent runtime, features and SDK. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Sandbox isolation is not per-tool isolation: tools in the same sandbox share its secrets and permitted egress destinations. MongoDB explicitly says it does not scope secrets or network access to individual tools. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Memory visibility is project-bounded: `org` means readable within the project, not across projects. Semantic, episodic, and procedural writes default to `private`, while taxonomic writes default to `org`. (medium confidence)

Trace content requires data governance: MongoDB’s agent-template repository warns that stored conversations and traces can contain database names, collection names, field names, and documents read by the agent. (low confidence)

Atlas Agent Engine offers a modular agent platform: customers can adopt a layer or the full stack. Independent analysis also describes component adoption as separable from a database architecture migration. (medium confidence)

Independent analysis recommends evaluating Agent Engine components independently and requiring an explicit compatibility map before coupling adoption to Atlas Infinite. Its architecture distinction is that a unified product announcement does not establish compatibility between every agent component and a newly announced database architecture. (low confidence)

Reusing a session ID reuses its reservation and session state; do not reuse IDs across workloads that require isolation. Scaling changes require rebuilding and redeploying because the platform snapshots them at build time. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

During Public Preview, the GitHub App and UI Connect Repository flow are unavailable; MongoDB directs users to run `agentengine deploy` from a local repository clone. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Within a project, agents share an Orchestration Engine that does not authenticate or authorize calling agents. MongoDB recommends separate projects when stronger agent isolation is required. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
Configured policies constrain execution; when no policy of a given type applies, the corresponding action remains unrestricted. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

The SDK documentation says bound `session_id` is inherited for conversation I/O but not for episodic or semantic search. Episodic search requires an explicit call argument for session filtering because consolidated episodes are session-unscoped. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The execution architecture separates agent graph execution from remote tool execution: local tools run in the agent process, while remote tool bodies run on demand in the Tool Sandbox or Tool Pod when OE routes them. (high confidence)

Install with `pip install agent-engine-sdk-memory` and import `Memory` and `MemoryRequestContext` from `agent_engine_sdk_memory`. The SDK documentation describes runtime dependencies limited to `pydantic` and `httpx`. (medium confidence)

The limitations page describes Orchestration Engine capacity as up to 50 concurrent requests per second across a project; it separately fixes agent resources at 0.5 vCPU and 2 GB, and Orchestration Engine resources at 0.5 vCPU and 512 MB. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A service account has exactly one role. Project accounts need `PROJECT_OWNER` to invoke agents; organization accounts need `ORG_GROUP_CREATOR` or `ORG_OWNER`. Read-only service accounts cannot invoke. A project account is restricted to its own project, and organization accounts to their own organization; `ORG_GROUP_CREATOR` invokes only in Agent Engine-managed projects, whereas `ORG_OWNER` also invokes in Atlas-backed projects. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Deployments do not autoscale. `scaling.replicas` fixes the sandbox count and concurrent-session capacity; each session reserves an agent sandbox and a tool sandbox. The field accepts 1–512 and defaults to 4; exhausted reservations cause a `pool full` invoke error. All agents in one project share the 512 ceiling. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Compute allocations are fixed: each agent has 0.5 vCPU and 2 GB RAM; each Orchestration Engine has 0.5 vCPU and 512 MB RAM. Users cannot configure these allocations. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Service-account management requires a signed-in user with the required role; a service-account access token cannot create, rotate, deactivate, or restrict service accounts. Project creation requires `PROJECT_OWNER`; organization creation requires `ORG_GROUP_CREATOR`. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Secret rotation retains the prior service-account secret for up to seven days or its earlier expiration. A second rotation or account deactivation revokes the prior secret immediately. Deactivation also causes existing access tokens to fail on their next request. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

SDK documentation says failed background extraction does not undo a successful turn write. Environmental failures get bounded retries; content-determined failures are recorded without retry. A stored memory that lacks an embedding can appear through text or hybrid retrieval but cannot appear through semantic-only retrieval. (medium confidence)

HyperFRAME Research cautions that persistent agent memory can retain mistaken conclusions, outdated preferences or sensitive information; this is an analyst risk assessment, not an observed incident in this service. (low confidence)
The Monitoring UI tracks invocation volume, error rates, token usage, memory activity, and resource consumption for a project and its workspaces. (low confidence)

Monitoring latency p50 and p95 include approval waiting time. Trace inspection distinguishes active execution from human review time, so approval delays require separate interpretation from slow execution. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Deployments use fixed sandbox capacity rather than autoscaling; each session reserves agent and tool sandboxes, and an exhausted pool can return `pool full`. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Service-account management requires a signed-in user with the required role, rather than a service-account token. Token IP restrictions do not restrict token issuance; deactivation invalidates existing tokens on their next request. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

For the official Atlas agent templates, Atlas authorizes the agent’s shared programmatic identity rather than each person chatting with it; the repository says custom clients do not support per-user OIDC sign-in. Give that identity only permissions every agent user should have. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

AgentenCode characterizes its evaluation as vendor-document analysis rather than an independent security test; its production-readiness and isolation cautions are not penetration-test results. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-28)

MongoDB describes Agent Engine retrieval as powered by Voyage AI, including embeddings and reranking; Codesprint repeats that vendor description rather than reporting an independent benchmark. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-30)

The documented content guardrail type is limited to `output_validation`, with regular-expression matching rather than an enumerated general-purpose safety-classifier suite. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Codesprint recommends retrieving action-driving transactional state from its authoritative system immediately before a decision or write; this is application design advice rather than an Agent Engine default. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-30)

MongoDB presents Agent Engine retrieval as powered by Voyage AI embeddings and reranking; Lemon Web repeats this description. These sources describe the feature, rather than independently measuring retrieval accuracy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-29)

Binding a request context creates a new scoped handle without changing the original. Identity resolves from call arguments, then bound context, then runtime context; blank values fall through rather than clearing a bound identity. (low confidence)

The shared runner is an internal dependency of framework SDKs rather than the package agent authors normally install; Python documentation names LangGraph and ADK adapters, while the TypeScript shared runner names its LangGraph adapter. (medium confidence)

Agent authors expose an in-process `App` object rather than implementing an HTTP endpoint. The Python contract uses `agent.yaml` to resolve a module attribute, registers graph construction with `@app.entrypoint`, and starts the application with `app.run()`. (low confidence)

Checkpoint state is separate from a live sandbox process: agent sandboxes are ephemeral, and MongoDB stores graph checkpoints between suspend and resume. Graph state must be JSON/BSON-serializable rather than containing live connections, file handles or unsupported custom objects. (low confidence)

MongoDB documents Atlas Agent Engine as Public Preview for evaluation and prototyping, discourages production workloads, and offers no platform-availability SLA or SLO during preview. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The `scaling.replicas` setting accepts 1–512 and defaults to 4; replicas across agents share a project-level ceiling of 512, so this is not a per-agent guarantee of 512 concurrently running agents. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The deployment CLI deploys the last successful build by default; `--build-id` selects a build, while `--version` selects the release build for an `agent.yaml` version. These selectors are mutually exclusive. `--auto` combines build and deployment monitoring for single-agent projects. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
Deployed agent code should write files only under `/tmp` or `/scratch`; MongoDB warns that other runtime paths may not be writable. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

For signed-in users, full agent management requires an explicit `Project Owner` assignment on the containing Atlas project. `Organization Owner` alone does not grant agent management, even though Atlas normally grants implicit project ownership; other project roles have read-only agent access. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
Secrets are stored in AWS Secrets Manager, default to project scope shared across workspaces, and can be restricted with `--workspace-scope`. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The `agentengine atlas setup` command grants `readWriteAnyDatabase` on the destination cluster. For narrower database access, MongoDB directs users to create a database user manually and supply a workspace-scoped `MONGODB_URI` limited to `MDB_AGENTIC_STORE_DB` and `MONGOMEM_DB_NAME`. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A workspace starts in `deny_all`, which still permits the base policy: DNS, services in the same namespace, and the linked Atlas cluster. Per-sandbox modes also include `allow_list` and `allow_all`. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A Project Member with read access can inspect deployed egress policies; editing a local policy needs no role, but deployment to apply it requires Project Owner. Policy changes take effect after redeployment. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
Secrets are capped at 100 per project and 100 per workspace. Exceeding these limits returns `400 Bad Request` with `RESOURCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Resource quotas include 25 workspaces, 100 credential providers, and 100 project service accounts per project, plus 100 organization service accounts per organization. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

MongoDB separately states an Orchestration Engine capacity of “up to 50 concurrent requests per second” across a project. This wording is a separate request-capacity restriction and must not be treated as a guarantee of 512 simultaneously usable sessions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A service-account IP access list restricts requests using its access token, but does not restrict token requests. Updating the list replaces it entirely; an empty list removes restrictions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Secrets are stored in AWS Secrets Manager. The CLI defaults to project-scoped secrets shared across workspaces; use `--workspace-scope` to restrict a secret to one workspace. Limits are 100 secrets per project and 100 per workspace. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Egress starts in `deny_all`, except the base policy permits DNS, same-namespace services, and the linked Atlas cluster. Policies are per sandbox and support `deny_all`, `allow_list`, and `allow_all`. An egress policy must be declared before deployment, and edits take effect only after redeployment by a Project Owner. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Preview API endpoints and formats can change without a compatible migration path. Pin an API contract in the `Accept` header on each request and follow-up read. Pinning preserves request and response shapes only; it does not freeze deployments, stored data, permissions, CLI/SDK releases, or model versions. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
Agent Engine discovers tools from configured remote MCP servers at startup and exposes them to agent code. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Agent code routes tool and model calls through `app.tool(...)` and `app.llm(...)` wrappers for auditing, policy enforcement and replay. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
The guardrail configuration exposes `llm_input` and `llm_output` stages, and `block`, `modify`, `log_only`, and `require_review` actions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Policy Engine allowlists restrict which tools and models an agent can call. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

A project with no effective policies runs without Policy Engine restrictions; policy enforcement should not be assumed to imply a preconfigured deny policy. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
The documented remote MCP transport is Streamable HTTP; the configuration schema identifies `streamable_http` as the only supported transport value. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Content guardrails and action policies are separate: guardrails inspect model content, while policies govern actions such as tool and model invocation. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

The policy engine supports tool-name and tool-catalog allowlisting; a catalog allowance also covers tools added to that catalog later. Custom tools without a catalog match by name. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Duration and token caps are checkpoint controls: a call can exceed the cap, and concurrent executions can collectively overshoot a session token cap. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Biagolini explicitly excludes guardrails and custom-tool construction from the hands-on walkthrough; it supplies no implementation validation for those features. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

MongoDB documents a persistent memory service that can run independently of an agent deployment; the standalone `agent-engine-sdk-memory` Python package records conversation turns and retrieves context for external applications. (medium confidence)
The SDK exposes a Memory facade and depends only on pydantic and httpx, avoiding a dependency on the full platform stack. (low confidence)

Memory has raw, chronological short-term conversation history and durable long-term knowledge. Background processing summarizes conversation snapshots and uses an LLM to extract semantic facts, episodic histories, procedural workflows, and taxonomic terms; applications can also write long-term memories directly. (medium confidence)

Background extraction processes conversation snapshots asynchronously. A successful turn write does not mean its extracted long-term knowledge is ready for the next turn; use short-term memory for recent conversational context. (medium confidence)

`build_context` and `build_context_from_sources` assemble prompt-ready context by ranking, de-duplicating, and budgeting matches; `search` and per-type searches return records. The default context sources are semantic and episodic; STM, procedural, and taxonomic sources require explicit inclusion. (medium confidence)

The per-source context builder accepts separate retrieval modes, filters and candidate counts. Semantic retrieval matches embeddings, text retrieval matches words, and hybrid retrieval combines their rankings. (low confidence)

Hosted standalone connections use a service-account access token and project identifier. Local development connects to the CLI-managed proxy using a base URL with no project identifier; platform-deployed agents instead receive a prewired Memory instance. (medium confidence)

The standalone guide supports custom memory types in hosted mode but excludes them locally. The SDK capability table likewise marks hosted custom-type `save` / `retrieve` as flag-gated, direct mode as unavailable without execution context, and app-bound mode as supported; unsupported operations raise `MemoryNotSupportedError`. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

The SDK reads and writes data but does not configure the memory server. Server settings live in the `memory:` block of `project-config.yaml`; `agentengine memory configure` stores them and `agentengine memory apply` restarts or provisions the runtime to read them. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

A MongoDB partner example documents using the SDK to connect externally hosted agents to the memory service, with extraction and storage performed server-side. This demonstrates an integration pattern, not independent production-performance validation. (low confidence)

The SDK exposes one `Memory` facade for both external and platform-hosted agents. An external application constructs it and binds conversation identity; a platform agent receives an instance whose invocation identity and transport are supplied by the runtime. (medium confidence)

`bind(ctx)` creates a new scoped handle without changing the original. `record_turn` uses the bound user and session and offers no per-call `user_id` or `visibility` override, so external applications should bind each conversation explicitly. (medium confidence)

`build_context_from_sources` accepts a `SourceSpec` per source with its own retrieval `mode`, `metadata_filter`, and `top_k`; modes are `text`, `semantic`, or `hybrid`. Its default mode is semantic, while the SDK recommends hybrid for text-bearing sources to combine paraphrase retrieval with exact-term matching. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The SDK documents `max_tokens` as a gross context-construction budget: it subtracts a 500-token formatting reserve and selects whole chunks from what remains. Positive budgets at or below 500 leave no room for memory chunks; larger budgets can still return empty context if no chunk fits. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

For SDK reads, `user_id` and `visibility` combine as an intersection. Passing `visibility="org"` on a user-bound handle does not union project knowledge with personal memory; the SDK recommends separate reads and merging for that use case. (medium confidence)

The memory guide says a deployed agent invoked using a service account uses that service account as its memory user identity and ignores invoke-supplied end-user IDs. It distinguishes the standalone memory service, which accepts explicit end-user and session IDs, and recommends that path for end-user isolation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Agent Engine records execution traces automatically; runs can be inspected for model calls, tool calls, timing, and errors. (medium confidence)

Native traces organize conversations into sessions, runs, and steps. The Playground shows the current user’s interactive sessions; Monitor > Traces covers project sessions across workspaces and invocation channels. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
Treat trace token totals as lower bounds: session totals omit some usage such as memory extraction, and active runs can undercount until steps finish. (low confidence)
Interpret health metrics carefully: invocations exclude runs waiting for approval, while latency percentiles include time spent waiting for approval. (low confidence)

Policy denial monitoring counts tool authorization and execution/session budget denials, but excludes model authorization denials; the displayed count is therefore not a complete count of every policy denial. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Runtime logs capture stdout/stderr, print statements, logging calls, and framework debug output; the runtime-log API supports filtering by execution and session IDs to correlate logs with traces. (medium confidence)
The Python runner architecture documents execution logging to JSONL and MongoDB plus OpenTelemetry tracing, including JSONL and MongoDB span exporters. (low confidence)
Arize documents an Agent Engine trace-export integration for observability and evaluation; Moor Insights also reports integrations with observability and evaluation providers. (medium confidence)

Arize’s integration article describes online evaluation of both final outputs and execution paths, annotation queues for failures, and reviewed examples becoming experimental datasets for comparing changes before redeployment. These are Arize AX capabilities described by the integration vendor. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Arize says its integration ingests OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and OpenInference, and accepts OTLP-emitting runtimes on Agent Engine without custom instrumentation code; this statement is conditional on the runtime already emitting OTLP. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Kegan Quimby characterizes the launch claims as lacking independent production evaluation and argues that independent customer evaluations would be more persuasive than launch testimonials; this is an attributed critique, not a benchmark result. (low confidence)

Agent Engine records execution traces automatically, including model/tool steps, timing, and token usage; Arize describes span-level inspection of this telemetry for debugging agent behavior. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

The Monitoring UI tracks project and workspace invocations, errors, tokens, memory activity, and resource usage, with selectable 1h, 24h, 7d, and 30d periods and automatic refresh every 60 seconds. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Interpret trace token totals as lower bounds: they omit some usage such as memory extraction. Session timeline token and memory totals also undercount while runs or steps remain unfinished. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Runtime logs capture stdout/stderr, print statements, logging calls, and framework debug output. Log entries expose executionId, sessionId, and traceId, supporting correlation between runtime logs and traces. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Arize’s published export instructions require customer mirroring, Full content, and Always on sampling. Full content sends prompts, completions, and tool payloads; verify the current export controls before enabling this configuration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The Runner SDK integrates the Agent Execution Runtime (AER), Tool Pod, and Memory Server; the Orchestration Engine (OE) is a separate service, with AER running agent logic and Tool Pod providing isolated tool execution. (low confidence)

The TypeScript runner-shared package supplies protocol handling, secure call wrappers, request-scoped context and server adapters; it is an open-source integration library, and does not distribute the managed OE or AER services. Agent authors install a framework SDK that depends on it. (low confidence)

Intercepted calls cross OE before execution. OE owns routing and returns the final outcome; remote tool calls use Tool Pod execution, while approved local calls return to the original AER call stack. (medium confidence)

The wrapper boundary limits the architecture’s guarantees: the Agent Contract states that calls outside `app.tool(...)` and `app.llm(...)` are not audited and do not replay correctly after resume. Universal governance or replay must not be inferred for arbitrary unwrapped application code. (low confidence)
The MongoDB agent templates illustrate the runtime split by running model and MCP calls in a tool sandbox separate from the agent. (low confidence)

The official pages give conflicting entrypoint-construction timings: Runner SDK architecture says tool application construction attempts the entrypoint during startup; Agent Contract says startup does not run the entrypoint and the Tool Sandbox loads it lazily on the first LLM invocation. These are attributed documentation positions, not a resolved statement of runtime behavior. (low confidence)

Resume combines graph checkpointing with OE-owned replay caching for wrapped operations. OE returns previously stored outcomes for replayed calls to avoid repeating their side effects; a cached response is distinct from executing a new call. (medium confidence)
